finite_witness: A single finite graph $G$ on $n \geq 12$ vertices whose chromatic symmetric function $X_G$ is Schur-positive but for which $X_G(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ fails SNP for some $k$ — i.e. a lattice point in the Newton polytope of $X_G(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ that is absent from its support.
gate_reason: Condition 1: a single graph settles the universal claim, since the conjecture is a for-all statement over graphs. Condition 2: checking terminates — compute $X_G$ (finite sum over stable partitions / expand in $m_\lambda$), expand in the Schur basis to test $s$-positivity, then for each $k$ compute the support, the convex hull of the support in $\mathbb{R}^k$, and enumerate its lattice points; all finite exact-arithmetic steps. Condition 3: graphs on $n$ vertices are enumerable (nauty/geng), and $k \leq n$ suffices since $X_G(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ stabilises.
frontier_quote: We also showed that in order to test Monical's conjecture one needs to consider graphs with $n\geq 12$ vertices (see \cite[Section 7.4]{MMS}).
frontier_search_space: All graphs on 12 vertices — roughly $1.7 \times 10^{11}$ up to isomorphism, and each candidate requires computing a degree-12 symmetric function, a Schur expansion, and lattice-point enumeration in polytopes up to dimension 12; the per-graph cost is what makes this hard, not just the count.
machinery_reason: The definitions (chromatic symmetric function, Schur expansion, Newton polytope, saturation) are all standard graduate-level algebraic combinatorics and are spelled out in the excerpt. No research programme must be absorbed to state or test the claim; the difficulty is computational, not conceptual. Some familiarity with $s$-positivity heuristics for $X_G$ (Gasharov's $P$-tableaux, incomparability graphs) helps target the search.
prior_computation_detail: The context reports results obtained by computation without pointing at reusable code: "showed in \cite[Example 7.5]{MMS} that a stronger notion than the SNP property called M-convexity does not hold" and "We also showed that in order to test Monical's conjecture one needs to consider graphs with $n\geq 12$ vertices (see \cite[Section 7.4]{MMS})" — the latter is almost certainly an exhaustive check up to 11 vertices, but no repository or tables are named here.
attention_reason: The context names Monical (2018 thesis conjecture), Adve--Robichaux--Yong, and the present authors with Selover, and describes concrete partial results: verification for claw-free incomparability graphs (Theorem 5.8 of MMS), failure of the stronger M-convexity property (Example 7.5), a computational clearance below 12 vertices (Section 7.4), and a complexity-theoretic tension argument with Stanley's claw-free conjecture. That is a handful of results over roughly seven years, not decades of concentrated effort — and crucially the computational clearance is recent, which is the kind of attention that does exhaust a search region.
argument: The object is concrete: one graph on $\geq 12$ vertices that is $s$-positive yet whose truncation $X_G(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ has a hole in its support. The paper hands you the starting line — everything below 12 vertices is already cleared — and it also hands you the most promising lead: the authors already broke M-convexity, the strictly stronger property, in Example 7.5, so the natural first move is to take their M-convexity counterexample, look at what near-miss structure produced the failure, and perturb toward an actual support gap rather than blind-enumerating $10^{11}$ twelve-vertex graphs. The strongest reason this eats a week for nothing is the verification cost rather than the count: each candidate needs an exact Schur expansion of a degree-12 symmetric function to certify $s$-positivity (the expensive and rare condition) before you even look at Newton polytopes, so any brute-force sweep must filter on $s$-positivity first, and $s$-positive graphs are sparse and awkward to generate directly. Two further cautions: the authors themselves write that this "makes it hard to find a counterexample," and the Adve--Robichaux--Yong complexity tension cuts both ways — it suggests a counterexample exists, but it says nothing about where, so a failed search yields no publishable structure.
